questions.q: Why write the model-selection rule (for example, 'ship logistic regression unless the forest wins by more than 0.02 AP') before running the tuning searches?
options: It makes the searches run faster
So you cannot bend the rule after seeing the results to justify a preferred model
Because scikit-learn requires a rule for GridSearchCV
So the test set can be used during tuning
questions.explain: Deciding the criterion in advance guards against motivated reasoning. Here tuning changed little, and the pre-set bar made the choice straightforward.

questions.q: The contact policy (top 10% by score) was chosen using out-of-fold probabilities from the training set. Why not choose it on the test set?
options: The test set is too small to contain any probabilities
Policies can only be computed from training data
Choosing it on the test set would make the test result optimistic, because the test data would have helped tune the decision
The test set has no labels
questions.explain: Anything selected using the test set is no longer an independent estimate. Out-of-fold training predictions let you choose the policy without touching it.

questions.q: With a contact cost of 15, a 30% save rate, and a saved customer worth 240, the break-even churn probability is 15 / (0.30 x 240) = 0.208. What does it mean?
options: Contacting a customer is worth it, on average, once their churn probability exceeds 0.208, under the illustrative costs
20.8% of customers will churn
The model's accuracy is 20.8%
The threshold must always be 0.5
questions.explain: The expected benefit of contacting a customer with churn probability p is p x 72 minus 15, which is positive above 0.208. These cost figures are illustrative assumptions, not measured values.

questions.q: Test precision in the top 10% was 0.405 with a 95% interval of 0.297 to 0.527. Why does this pass the minimum-viable criterion from lesson 3?
options: Because the point estimate is above 0.4
Because bootstrap intervals are always valid
Because the interval's width is under 0.5
Because the lower end of the interval (0.297) is above the 0.208 break-even, so even a pessimistic reading still pays
questions.explain: Lesson 3 required the lower end of the bootstrap interval, not just the point estimate, to clear the break-even. The interval is wide because only 74 customers are flagged.

questions.q: Under the illustrative economics, contacting everyone had a net value of about -3,878 per 1,000 customers while contacting the top 10% earned about +1,423. Why does contacting everyone lose money?
options: Because the model is uncalibrated
Because only 15.4% of all customers churn, below the 20.8% break-even precision, so the average contact costs more than it earns
Because the offer never works
Because contacting more customers always lowers precision to zero
questions.explain: Precision among all customers equals the base rate of 15.4%. Below 20.8% each contact loses money on average; the model earns value by concentrating contacts on customers above the break-even.
